Let me ask you this question. Looking at this map, where is the most strategically located place? It's here, right? This is in the center of global trade and where human civilization began. We call it Samaria, okay? Writing was invented there, and a lot of trade happened because Samaria connects everyone to everyone else. If you're in a civilization and want to get through Egypt, you have to transport your goods to Samaria first, which then overland takes it to Egypt. Same thing if you want to reach everywhere else.

Samaria was the first major civilization where they invented writing, irrigation, and other technologies. Historians debate the language spoken by Samarans because it's different from surrounding areas. One theory is that people came together in this area to trade and formed their own language. Scholars are surprised at Samaria's rapid development, possibly due to alien visitors called the Anunnaki, though that’s a stupid idea.

Necessity is the mother of creativity, so they created their writing system when coming together to trade. If you put different people on an island, they would quickly develop their own language and civilization because necessity drives invention. So, in this class, we'll talk about how civilization development promotes writing and mythology. Studying mythology can reveal lost history.

One principle of human history is that it's a constant process of inversion. During the caping era, society was egalitarian, fluid, and animistic. Agriculture introduced the mother goddess for fertility. As societies grew larger and started warring with each other, males overtook females, and they began worshipping sky gods instead. With hereditary societies, civil wars occur where princes kill kings. Over time, as populations increased, a bureaucracy emerged, leading servants to collude against kings. History is a constant process of inversion, with old orders being dethroned by new ones.
